gaps: Who may apply: § 4-202(a) speaks of "a person or governmental unit" with no residency or purpose limit, and § 4-203(c)(2) bars ignoring an application on the ground that it was meant to harass. The custodian, the official custodian and "the Board" are defined elsewhere in Title 4 (not in the modelled sections); the model uses one custodian lane for both custodian roles.

Written application (§ 4-202(b)): no written application is needed for records an official custodian has listed under § 4-201(c)(2) or when the custodian waives the requirement. The model shows only the written path; the waiver and the listed-records route would rejoin at the custodian's decision.

Wrong recipient (§ 4-202(c)) and nonexistent record (§ 4-202(d)) are modelled as exclusive alternatives to the custodian's grant-or-deny decision, reached directly from the application. § 4-202(d) requires notice immediately when the custodian concludes on initial review that no record exists, and otherwise promptly after the search but within 30 days; only the 30-day outer limit is a timer. The text does not say what a missed 10-working-day referral notice or 30-day no-record notice leads to, so both timers end at an implied 'deadline missed' state.

Grant or deny (§ 4-203(a)): 30 days after receiving the application (50 days for an application that is the subject of § 4-356; only the 30-day figure is shown). The section does not say what a missed grant-or-deny deadline means; only a failure to produce an approved record is declared a denial (§ 4-203(b)(3)), so the timer on decide_application ends at an implied end state rather than deemed_denied.

Deemed denial (§ 4-203(b)(3)): a failure to produce the record "in accordance with this subsection" is a denial, modelled by routing the 30-day production timer to deemed_denied. The text adds that such a denial may not be treated as the result of a bona fide dispute unless the custodian gave the (b)(2) delay notice and is working with the applicant in good faith; that qualification affects later remedies and is not modelled.

Delay notice (§ 4-203(b)(2)): required within 10 working days of receipt when the custodian reasonably believes production will take more than 10 working days, and must give the anticipated time, an estimate of the range of fees, and the reason for the delay. Missing it is not said to end anything, so its timer rejoins the production step (on_miss produce_record). The model routes from the decision by exclusive gateway, so a denial and a delay notice cannot both be shown; the 30-day production limit in (b)(1) still applies on the face of the text even after a delay notice.

Denial (§ 4-203(c)(1)): the written statement is due "within 10 working days" without saying from when; the timer anchor is assumed to be the denial. The statement must give the reasons, the legal authority, a description of the withheld record that lets the applicant assess the authority, and notice of the review remedies, plus, for § 4-343 denials, why the denial is necessary and why redaction would not address the reasons. A partial denial is modelled as a denial followed by inspection of the remaining parts.

Extensions (§ 4-203(d)): any time limit in § 4-203 may be extended by up to 30 days with the applicant's consent, and is extended while a dispute under Subtitle 1A or 1B is pending. Neither extension is drawn as a step; the timers show the unextended periods.

Fees (§ 4-206): the official custodian may charge a reasonable fee (one bearing a reasonable relationship to actual costs) for search, preparation and reproduction, with staff and attorney review costs prorated by salary and time; the first 2 hours of search and preparation are free; another law that sets a copy fee applies instead; and the cost of reproduction facilities the custodian lacked may be charged. The text does not say when the fee is charged relative to production, so charge_fee is placed after produce_record. Waiver needs a request plus either indigency with an affidavit (household income under 50% of the State median) or a public-interest finding; the waiver is discretionary ('may'), so waiver_permitted only allows it. For a local school system, the custodian must tell the applicant they may complain to the Board about the fee; waive_fee and school_fee_notice are shown as exclusive alternatives although both could apply.

This is the Maryland Public Information Act process; it governs requests to Maryland state agencies and to Baltimore and other Maryland local governments. Requests in Virginia (Va. Code § 2.2-3704) or the District of Columbia follow their own statutes and are modelled separately.
